claim: GFE3 is a protein that can ablate inhibitory synapses efficiently, rapidly, and without toxicity by targeting an E3 ligase to the scaffolding protein Gephyrin.
source: Previously, we developed GFE3, a protein that can ablate inhibitory synapses efficiently, rapidly, and without toxicity by targeting an E3 ligase to the scaffolding protein Gephyrin (Gross et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gross et al., 2016, which is prior published work.

claim: GFE3 consists of GPHN.FingR fused to the RING domain of the E3 ligase XIAP.
source: GFE3 consists of GPHN.FingR (Fibronectin intrabody generated by mRNA display), a recombinant, antibody-like protein, which binds Gephyrin at inhibitory synapses (Prior et al., 1992; Gross et al., 2013) fused to the RING domain of the E3 ligase XIAP (RINGXIAP) (Wilkinson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Prior et al., 1992, Gross et al., 2013, and Wilkinson et al., 2008.

claim: GFE3 mediates the ubiquitination of Gephyrin and disassembly of inhibitory synapses.
source: GFE3 mediates the ubiquitination of Gephyrin and disassembly of inhibitory synapses.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: GFE3 specifically targets postsynaptic sites containing GABAA receptors.
source: Importantly, it specifically targets postsynaptic sites containing GABAA receptors and can be expressed in genetically determined cell types.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: GFE3 has been used to probe the contribution of inhibitory inputs to LTP in hippocampal circuits.
source: GFE3 has been used to probe the contribution of inhibitory inputs to LTP in hippocampal circuits (Davenport et al., 2021), recurrent loops in the oscillator that drives rhythmic whisking (Golomb et al., 2022; Takatoh et al., 2022), and the temporal coordination of vocalization and inspiration (Park et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davenport et al., 2021, Golomb et al., 2022, Takatoh et al., 2022, and Park et al., 2024.

claim: No tool analogous to GFE3 that ablates excitatory synapses currently exists.
source: However, no tool analogous to GFE3 that ablates excitatory synapses currently exists.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: GFE3 is constitutively active, limiting its temporal and spatial resolution.
source: Furthermore, because GFE3 is constitutively active, its temporal and spatial resolution is limited.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: PFE3 is an excitatory synapse ablator.
source: In this study, we generated three tools for ablating synapses based on GFE3: (1) PFE3, an excitatory synapse ablator; (2) paGFE3, a photoactivatable version of GFE3; (3) chGFE3, a chemically activated version of GFE3.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: paGFE3 is a photoactivatable version of GFE3.
source: In this study, we generated three tools for ablating synapses based on GFE3: (1) PFE3, an excitatory synapse ablator; (2) paGFE3, a photoactivatable version of GFE3; (3) chGFE3, a chemically activated version of GFE3.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: chGFE3 is a chemically activated version of GFE3.
source: In this study, we generated three tools for ablating synapses based on GFE3: (1) PFE3, an excitatory synapse ablator; (2) paGFE3, a photoactivatable version of GFE3; (3) chGFE3, a chemically activated version of GFE3.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: Expression of PFE3 in cultured neurons causes the loss of PSD-95 puncta and excitatory synapses.
source: We show that the expression of PFE3 in cultured neurons causes the loss of PSD-95 puncta and excitatory synapses, which is reversible.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of PFE3 on excitatory synapses is reversible.
source: We show that the expression of PFE3 in cultured neurons causes the loss of PSD-95 puncta and excitatory synapses, which is reversible.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of PFE3 in vivo leads to the functional loss of excitatory synaptic transmission.
source: In vivo, its expression leads to the functional loss of excitatory synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: paGFE3 was generated by incorporating GPHN.FingR and the RINGXIAP into a novel photoactivatable complex based on the photocleavable protein PhoCl2c.
source: We generated paGFE3 by incorporating GPHN.FingR and the RINGXIAP into a novel photoactivatable complex based on the photocleavable protein PhoCl2c (Lu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2021 and Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: paGFE3 is activated by 400 nm light.
source: paGE3 is activated by 400 nm light and causes ablation of inhibitory synapses within 5 hr of exposure that is subsequently reversible.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: paGFE3 causes ablation of inhibitory synapses within 5 hr of exposure to 400 nm light.
source: paGE3 is activated by 400 nm light and causes ablation of inhibitory synapses within 5 hr of exposure that is subsequently reversible.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of paGFE3 on inhibitory synapses is reversible.
source: paGE3 is activated by 400 nm light and causes ablation of inhibitory synapses within 5 hr of exposure that is subsequently reversible.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: paGFE3 has no background activity in the absence of 400 nm light.
source: In the absence of 400 nm light, paGFE3 has no background activity.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of paGFE3 labels inhibitory synapses, allowing their size and location to be monitored before and after ablation.
source: In addition, the expression of paGFE3 labels inhibitory synapses, allowing their size and location to be monitored before and after ablation.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: chGFE3 mediates efficient, reversible degradation of labeled synapses when a cell-permeant chemical is added.
source: chGFE3, a chemogenetic version of GFE3 analogous to paGFE3, mediates efficient, reversible degradation of labeled synapses when a cell-permeant chemical is added.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PSD-95.FingR binds at high affinity and specificity to the scaffolding protein PSD-95.
source: Initially, to generate an excitatory synapse ablator, we fused RINGXIAP to PSD-95.FingR, which binds at high affinity and specificity to the scaffolding protein PSD-95, which is found at excitatory synapses (Hunt et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hunt et al., 1996.

claim: PSD-95 is found at excitatory synapses.
source: Initially, to generate an excitatory synapse ablator, we fused RINGXIAP to PSD-95.FingR, which binds at high affinity and specificity to the scaffolding protein PSD-95, which is found at excitatory synapses (Hunt et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hunt et al., 1996.

claim: PSD-95.FingR-RINGXIAP did not efficiently ablate PSD-95.
source: However, PSD-95.FingR-RINGXIAP did not efficiently ablate PSD-95 (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text, though the supporting data is not shown.

claim: The RING domain of the E3 ligase Mdm2 is necessary for PSD-95 degradation and excitatory synapse ablation during homeostatic plasticity.
source: As an alternative, we fused PSD-95.FingR to the RING domain of the E3 ligase Mdm2 (RINGMdm2), which is necessary for PSD-95 degradation and excitatory synapse ablation during homeostatic plasticity (Colledge et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Colledge et al., 2003.

claim: Co-expression of PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 with PSD-95-myc in COS7 cells reduced PSD-95-myc expression by approximately 50%.
source: Cells transfected with PSD-95 alone had a PSD-95-myc expression level of 203 ± 32 au, as measured by western blot, while the expression level of PSD-95 in cells co-expressing PSD-95-myc and PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 reduced to 107 ± 12 au, a ~50% decrease (n = 5, p < 0.05, ANOVA with multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Addition of the ubiquitination inhibitor TAK243 to cells co-expressing PSD-95-myc and PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 increased PSD-95 expression levels to 239 ± 31 au.
source: To determine whether this reduction in PSD-95 was due to ubiquitination, we tried a third condition, where the ubiquitination inhibitor TAK243 (Majeed et al., 2022) was added to cells co-expressing PSD-95-myc and PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2. In this case, PSD-95 expression levels increased to 239 ± 31 au, a ~20% increase relative to cells expressing PSD-95-myc alone, which was not significant (n = 5, p > 0.6, ANOVA with multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A, B, and is supported by a citation to Majeed et al., 2022.

claim: Cells co-expressing PSD-95-myc and PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 without TAK243 had approximately 55% less PSD-95 compared to those with TAK243.
source: Furthermore, cells co-expressing PSD-95-myc and PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 without TAK243 had ~55% less PSD-95 vs. those with TAK243, a significant difference (p < 0.05, ANOVA with multiple comparisons, Figure 1A, B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: TAK243 blocks ubiquitination.
source: To test whether TAK243 was blocking ubiquitination, we compared western blot staining of lysates from COS7 cells expressing Ubiquitin-HA with and without TAK243. Staining with anti-HA showed a distinctive laddering pattern in the lane corresponding to cells expressing Ubiquitin-HA without TAK243 consistent with ubiquitination, whereas the lanes corresponding to cells expressing Ubiquitin-HA with TAK243 and a control lane with lysate from untransfected cells showed no staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming that TAK243 blocks ubiquitination.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 degrades exogenously expressed PSD-95 through ubiquitination in COS7 cells.
source: Together, our results are consistent with PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 degrading exogenously expressed PSD-95 through ubiquitination in COS7 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP efficiently labels endogenous PSD-95.
source: Note that PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP efficiently labels endogenous PSD-95, allowing its spatial distribution to be mapped in real time in living cells (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gross et al., 2013.

claim: Transcriptional regulation matches the expression level of PSD-95.FingR with that of endogenous PSD-95.
source: Furthermore, transcriptional regulation matches the expression level of PSD-95.FingR with that of endogenous PSD-95, facilitating labeling with very low background.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: Induction of PSD-95.FingR-HA-RINGMdm2 expression with Dox reduced PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP labeling by 85%.
source: We found that PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP labeling was reduced by 85% (p = 0.002, Wilcoxon, n = 9 cells, 3 independent experiments, Figure 1C, D), consistent with efficient ablation of endogenous PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Expression of PSD-95.FingR-HA-RINGMdm2 reduced the number of puncta labeled with immunostaining of endogenous PSD-95 by 52%.
source: However, when we counted the number of puncta labeled with PSD-95.FingR at T0 and compared that to the number of puncta labeled with immunostaining of endogenous PSD-95 in the same cells at the end of the experiment, it showed a reduction of only 52% (Figure 1E, F, p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney, n = 9 cells, 3 independent experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: Efficient synapse elimination requires a combination of ubiquitination mediated by Mdm2 and interaction with the proteasome mediated by Protocadherin 10.
source: These findings were corroborated when we found efficient degradation of PSD-95 and ablation of synapses was only achieved if all three components were included in PFE3.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: PCDH 10 is a Ca2+-dependent cell adhesion protein that binds to both PSD-95 and the proteasome via its proteasome-interacting region (PIR).
source: PCDH 10 is a Ca2+-dependent cell adhesion protein that binds to both PSD-95 and the proteasome via its proteasome-interacting region (PIR) (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: Adding the PIR domain to the PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 complex might increase the efficiency with which PSD-95 is ablated.
source: Therefore, we reasoned that adding the PIR domain to the PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2 complex might increase the efficiency with which PSD-95 is ablated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PFE3 is PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2-PIR.
source: We generated a new protein, PSD-95.FingR-RINGMdm2-PIR, which we called PFE3.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: Expression of PFE3 reduced the labeling of PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP by 65%.
source: By comparing images at T0 and 48 hr, we found that the expression of PFE3 reduced the labeling of PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP by 65%, a significant difference (Figure 2A, B, D, n = 14 cells, 3 distinct experiments, p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2A, B, D.

claim: Dox-inducible PFE3 reduced the number of endogenous PSD-95 puncta by 73%.
source: When we checked these results by counting PSD-95 puncta labeled with PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP at T0 and immunocytochemistry against endogenous PSD-95 at 48 hr (Figure 2C), we found that Dox-inducible PFE3 reduced the number of endogenous PSD-95 puncta by 73% (Figure 2D, p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: Expression of RandE3 did not significantly affect PSD-95.FingR labeling.
source: As a control, we induced RandE3 (Random.FingR-RINGMdm2-PIR), which contained a fibronectin scaffold with a random binding pocket instead of PSD-95.FingR (Gross et al., 2016). The expression of RandE3 did not significantly affect PSD-95.FingR labeling (an increase of 30%, p > 0.1, Mann–Whitney, n = 8, 3 independent experiments) or the number of endogenous PSD-95 puncta (an increase of 2%, p > 0.9, Mann–Whitney, n = 8, 3 independent experiments, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D, and is supported by a citation to Gross et al., 2016.

claim: 89 ± 1% of PSD-95 puncta in non-transfected cultured cortical neurons were positive for GluA1.
source: We immunostained non-transfected cultured cortical neurons for PSD-95 and GluA1, a subunit of the AMPAR, and found that 89 ± 1% of PSD-95 puncta were positive for GluA1 (Figure 2E, H, 7570 synapses, 11 cells, 3 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2E, H.

claim: Neurons expressing RandE3 showed no significant change in the percentage of PSD-95-positive synapses labeled with GluA1 compared to control neurons.
source: Neurons co-transfected with the PSD-95.FingR and TRE-RandE3-HA and induced with Dox for 48 hr showed no significant change in the percentage of PSD-95-positive synapses labeled with GluA1 compared to control neurons (Figure 2F, H, 87 ± 2%, 3131 synapses, 9 cells, 2 experiments, p > 0.05, Kruskal–Wallis multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2F, H.

claim: Only 41 ± 5% of the remaining PSD-95 puncta in PFE3-expressing cells also contained GluA1.
source: Quantification of GluA1 in PFE3-expressing cells showed that only 41 ± 5% (1341 synapses, 10 cells, 2 experiments) of the remaining PSD-95 puncta also contained GluA1, a significant decrease from untransfected cells (Figure 2G, H, p < 0.001, Kruskal–Wallis multiple comparisons) and RandE3-expressing cells (p < 0.01, Kruskal–Wallis multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2G, H.

claim: PFE3 decreases the amount of GluA1 by approximately 90%.
source: Based on our result that PFE3 decreases PSD-95 puncta by 73% (Figure 2D) and that only 41% of the remaining puncta are positive for GluA1, we estimate that PFE3 decreases the amount of GluA1 by approximately 90%.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PFE3 mediates a significant reduction in both PSD-95 and GluA1.
source: Thus, our experiments are consistent with PFE3 mediating a significant reduction in both PSD-95 and GluA1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AMPARs are the predominant ionotropic glutamate receptor responsible for excitatory transmission.
source: Furthermore, because AMPARs are the predominant ionotropic glutamate receptor responsible for excitatory transmission (Gouaux, 2004), our results suggest that PFE3 reduces functional excitatory connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gouaux, 2004.

claim: PFE3 reduces functional excitatory connectivity.
source: Furthermore, because AMPARs are the predominant ionotropic glutamate receptor responsible for excitatory transmission (Gouaux, 2004), our results suggest that PFE3 reduces functional excitatory connectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and is supported by a citation to Gouaux, 2004.

claim: GFE3 degrades itself.
source: To test whether the ablation of excitatory synapses by PFE3 is reversible, we used a previous paradigm for testing GFE3. There, we found that because GFE3 degrades itself, it is sufficient to merely cease the induction of GFE3 expression to reverse its effect (Gross et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gross et al., 2016.

claim: Induction of PFE3 reduced PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP labeling by 81 ± 5%.
source: We found that, as in previous experiments, the induction of PFE3 reduced PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP labeling (−81 ± 5%, Figure 2I, J, L, p < 0.01, Friedman multiple comparison) and PSD-95.FingR puncta (−80 ± 5%, p < 0.01, Friedman multiple comparison, n = 8 cells, 4 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2I, J, L.

claim: Five days following removal of Dox, PSD-95.FingR labeling increased by 450 ± 100%.
source: Five days following removal of Dox, PSD-95.FingR labeling increased by 450 ± 100%, which was significant (Figure 2J–L, p < 0.01, Friedman multiple comparison) and the number of PSD-95.FingR puncta increased by 400 ± 65% (p < 0.05, Friedman multiple comparison).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2J–L.

claim: PSD-95.FingR labeling was not significantly different before adding Dox vs. after its removal.
source: PSD-95.FingR labeling was not significantly different before adding Dox vs. after its removal (Figure 2L, −10 ± 20%, p > 0.5, Friedman multiple comparison).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The number of PSD-95.FingR puncta did not show a significant change before induction of PFE3 vs. after its removal.
source: Similarly, the number of PSD-95.FingR puncta did not show a significant change before induction of PFE3 vs. after its removal (−11 ± 18%, p > 0.9, Friedman multiple comparison).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Endogenous PSD-95 is found on dendritic spines following synapse regrowth.
source: Furthermore, immunocytochemistry of neurons following incubation with Dox-free media showed that endogenous PSD-95 is found on dendritic spines following synapse regrowth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP puncta showed a similar distribution overall before and after ablation.
source: Finally, PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP puncta showed a similar distribution overall before and after ablation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: PSD-95 degradation by PFE3 is reversible.
source: These results are consistent with PSD-95 degradation by PFE3 being reversible.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons expressing RandE3 showed no significant change in the total PSD-95.FingR labeling before and after induction of RandE3 for 48 hr.
source: In a control experiment with RandE3, neurons showed no significant change in the total PSD-95.FingR labeling (+8 ± 6%, p > 0.9, Friedman test multiple comparison, n = 13, 2 experiments) or the number of PSD-95.FingR puncta (+8 ± 6%, p > 0.9, Friedman test multiple comparison) before and after induction of RandE3 for 48 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: PSD-95 degradation only occurs when the RINGMdm2-PIR domains are targeted by PSD-95.FingR.
source: Thus, PSD-95 degradation only occurs when the RINGMdm2-PIR domains are targeted by PSD-95.FingR.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cotransfection with PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP and TRE-PFE3-P2A-GFP without exposure to Dox results in labeling of PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP that is not significantly different from labeling in cultures transfected with PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP alone.
source: Finally, cotransfection with PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP and TRE-PFE3-P2A-GFP without exposure to Dox results in labeling of PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP that is not significantly different from labeling in cultures transfected with PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP alone, both in terms of total PSD-95.FingR-tagRFP labeling (p > 0.2, Mann–Whitney) and the number of labeled puncta (p > 0.4, Mann–Whitney, Figure 2—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Type 6 cone bipolar cells provide approximately 70% of the total synaptic input to On α-RGCs.
source: Synaptic currents were evoked by optogenetic stimulation of type 6 bipolar cells, which provide approximately 70% of the total synaptic input to On α-RGCs (Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2012.

claim: At a holding potential of –60 mV, synaptic currents from type 6 bipolar cells to On α-RGCs are almost purely AMPAergic.
source: At a holding potential of –60 mV, these synaptic currents are almost purely AMPAergic, as the AMPAR antagonist DNQX blocks the response (Tien et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tien et al., 2017.

claim: RGCs infected with the PFE3 virus had EPSCs with >80% reduction in amplitude compared to RGCs infected with the control virus.
source: Compared to RGCs infected with the control virus, RGCs infected with the PFE3 virus had EPSCs with >80% reduction in amplitude, 79 ± 30 pA (n = 9 cells, 5 mice) vs. 445 ± 78 pA (n = 8 cells, 3 mice), a significant difference (p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney, Figure 3B–D), which is consistent with a reduction in postsynaptic receptor density.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: PFE3 expression leads to the degradation of PSD-95, which reduces the number of AMPA receptors at excitatory synapses, causing a reduction in synaptic transmission.
source: Overall, our results are consistent with PFE3 expression leading to the degradation of PSD-95, which, in turn, reduces the number of AMPA receptors at excitatory synapses, causing a reduction in synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Existing photodimerization systems, such as the Cryptochrome (Cry2) system, have substantial background activity leading to loss of inhibitory synapses even in the dark.
source: To generate a photoactivatable version of GFE3 to ablate inhibitory synapses, we first used existing photodimerization systems, such as the Cryptochrome (Cry2) system, but we found them to have substantial background activity leading to loss of inhibitory synapses even in the dark (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PhoCl undergoes cleavage when exposed to violet (~400 nm) light.
source: PhoCl undergoes cleavage when exposed to violet (~400 nm) light, creating two peptides, the C-terminal 10 amino acids, including the chromophore, and the remainder of the protein, referred to as the 'empty barrel' (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: Following photocleavage, a novel epitope is exposed on the empty barrel of PhoCl.
source: Following photocleavage, a novel epitope is exposed on the empty barrel.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: PhLIC consists of the empty barrel and a 10-mer peptide called PhoCl-binding peptide (PBP) that binds to the empty barrel but not to full-length PhoCl.
source: Based on this property of PhoCl, we developed a photoactivatable complex, PhLIC (PhoCl-based Light-Inducible Complex), consisting of the empty barrel and a 10-mer peptide called PhoCl-binding peptide (PBP) that binds to the empty barrel but not to full-length PhoCl (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: PhoCl does not undergo cleavage in the dark or ambient light.
source: Because PhoCl does not undergo cleavage in the dark or ambient light (Zhang et al., 2017), there should be no background formation of PhLIC.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: mRNA display was used to create binders to synaptic proteins.
source: To generate PBP, we used the in vitro directed evolution technique, mRNA display, which we have used to create binders to synaptic proteins (Gross et al., 2013; Mora et al., 2013; Roberts and Szostak, 1997; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gross et al., 2013, Mora et al., 2013, and Roberts and Szostak, 1997.

claim: PBPs bound to cleaved PhoCl in COS7 cells but not in neurons after the first selection.
source: Following the first selection, which lasted six rounds, we found PBPs bound to cleaved PhoCl in COS7 cells but not in neurons (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text, though the supporting data is not shown.

claim: PBP pulled down photocleaved PhoCl2c, but not full-length PhoCl2c.
source: We found that PBP pulled down photocleaved PhoCl2c, but not full-length PhoCl2c (Figure 4B), suggesting that PhLIC could act as a photoactivatable system with low background.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PhoCl2c is an improved version of the original PhoCl containing five mutations and with faster and more efficient cleavage.
source: Note that PhoCl2c is an improved version of the original PhoCl containing five mutations and with faster and more efficient cleavage (Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2021.

claim: Following exposure to 400 nm light for 1 min and incubation in the dark for 3 hr, PBP-tagRFP became 3.3 ± 0.5 times more concentrated in the area colocalized with GTS-PhoCl2c staining than vs. the rest of the cell.
source: Following exposure to 400 nm light for 1 min and incubation in the dark for 3 hr, PBP-tagRFP became 3.3 ± 0.5 times more concentrated in the area colocalized with GTS-PhoCl2c staining than vs. the rest of the cell, a significant difference (p < 0.001, n = 11, Wilcoxon, 2 experiments, Figure 4D, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 4D, F.

claim: Exposure to ambient light did not affect the localization of PBP-tagRFP.
source: Note that exposure to ambient light did not affect the localization of PBP-tagRFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E), and exposing cells transfected only with tagRFP to 400 nm did not affect the localization of tagRFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: PhLIC shows robust activation upon exposure to 400 nm light but no activation in ambient light.
source: These experiments suggest that PhLIC shows robust activation upon exposure to 400 nm light but no activation in ambient light.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c is targeted to inhibitory synapses and acts as an anchor that recruits PBP-E3 once PhoCl2c has been cleaved.
source: Note that tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c performs two functions. It is targeted to inhibitory synapses, where it acts as an anchor that recruits PBP-E3 once PhoCl2c has been cleaved.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c acts as a label, allowing inhibitory synapses to be visualized before and after PhCl2c is cleaved.
source: It also acts as a label, allowing inhibitory synapses to be visualized before and after PhCl2c is cleaved (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl labels inhibitory synapses.
source: To test whether paGFE3 labels inhibitory synapses, we expressed tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl in cortical neurons in culture and co-labeled tagRFP and endogenous Gephyrin. The two labels are colocalized, consistent with tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl labeling inhibitory synapses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: paGFE3 does not cause background degradation of inhibitory synapses.
source: To test if paGFE3 caused background degradation of inhibitory synapses, we compared cultured cortical neurons transfected with paGFE3 (transcriptionally regulated tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl and PBP-E3) with similar neurons transfected with tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl alone and incubated for 5 days. Quantification of tagRFP labeling showed an 8% reduction, which was not significant (n = 10 cells, 1 experiment, p > 0.4, Mann–Whitney, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with no background degradation of Gephyrin in the dark.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When Cry2-tagRFP-GPHN.FingR and CIB1-RINGXIAP were co-transfected into cultured cortical neurons and incubated for 5 days, tagRFP labeling was 48% less than when GPHN.FingR-Cry2-tagRFP was transfected by itself.
source: In contrast, when Cry2-tagRFP-GPHN.FingR and CIB1-RINGXIAP were co-transfected into cultured cortical neurons and incubated for 5 days, tagRFP labeling was 48% less than when GPHN.FingR-Cry2-tagRFP was transfected by itself (650 ± 90 au, n = 10 cells, 1 experiment vs. 1250 ± 110 au, n = 9 cells, 1 experiment), a significant difference (p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells expressing paGFE3 showed a 61 ± 3% reduction in tagRFP labeling 5 hr after exposure to 400 nm light.
source: The neurons showed a 61 ± 3% reduction in tagRFP labeling (130 ± 9 vs. 52 ± 6 a.u., a significant difference, p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, n = 17 cells, 3 experiments, Figure 5B–E) and a 40 ± 6% drop in the number of GPHN.FingR puncta (268 ± 24 vs. 161 ± 20 puncta), a significant change (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, n = 17, 3 experiments, Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: Cells expressing transcriptionally regulated tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c without PBP-RING had a much smaller reduction in labeling (10 ± 2%) when exposed to 400 nm light.
source: Importantly, cells expressing transcriptionally regulated tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c without PBP-RING had a much smaller reduction in labeling (10 ± 2%, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E) when exposed to 400 nm light as above, although it was statistically significant (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, n = 14 cells, 3 experiments, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: The number of GPHN.FingR-labeled puncta did not show a significant change in cells expressing tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c without PBP-RING when exposed to 400 nm light.
source: However, the number of GPHN.FingR-labeled puncta did not show a significant change (0.4 ± 2%, p > 0.7, Wilcoxon, n = 14 cells, 3 experiments, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating the reduction in total GPHN.FingR labeling is likely a result of photobleaching and not due to the decrease in Gephyrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells expressing paGFE3 undergo efficient degradation of Gephyrin puncta when exposed to 400 nm light.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with cells expressing paGFE3 undergoing efficient degradation of Gephyrin puncta when exposed to 400 nm light.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The PhLIC-GFE3 complexes are self-degrading.
source: We reasoned that the PhLIC-GFE3 complexes would be self-degrading, as was GFE3.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The total fluorescence from the tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c label was reduced by 63 ± 5% between T0 and +5 hr after exposure to 400 nm light.
source: Comparing the images, we found the total fluorescence from the tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c label was reduced by 63 ± 5% between T0 and +5 hr, then increased by 130 ± 28% between +5 hr and +4 days, a significant difference (p < 0.001 for T0 to +5 hr; p < 0.05, +5 hr to +4 days, Friedman test, multiple comparisons, n = 9 cells, 2 experiments, Figure 5F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5F–I.

claim: There was a 20 ± 9% decrease in tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c labeling from T0 to +4 days, which was not significant.
source: In addition, there was a 20 ± 9% decrease from T0 to +4 days, which was not significant (p > 0.1, Friedman test, multiple comparisons, Figure 5I), suggesting that paGFE3 is reversible.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5I.

claim: paGFE3 is reversible.
source: In addition, there was a 20 ± 9% decrease from T0 to +4 days, which was not significant (p > 0.1, Friedman test, multiple comparisons, Figure 5I), suggesting that paGFE3 is reversible.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Puncta before and after ablation with paGFE3 were in similar locations.
source: We also found that puncta before and after ablation were in similar locations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: paGFE3 can mediate light-inducible degradation of endogenous Gephyrin that has virtually no background and is reversible.
source: Together, our results indicate that paGFE3 can mediate light-inducible degradation of endogenous Gephyrin that has virtually no background and is reversible.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: chGFE3 is based on a chemically induced dimerization system based on E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (eDHFR) and the HaloTag protein.
source: We used a chemically induced dimerization system based on E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (eDHFR) and the HaloTag protein.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: When combined with the small molecule TH, eDHFR and HaloTag form a bio-orthogonal complex in eukaryotic cells.
source: When combined with the small molecule TH, a fusion of trimethoprim (TMP) and HaloTag ligand, eDHFR and HaloTag form a bio-orthogonal complex in eukaryotic cells (Ballister et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ballister et al., 2014.

claim: The formation of the eDHFR-HaloTag complex is reversible because the binding of eDHFR to TMP is not covalent and can be outcompeted by adding excess TMP.
source: Furthermore, the formation of the complex is reversible because the binding of eDHFR to TMP is not covalent and can be outcompeted by adding excess TMP.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-HaloTag labels inhibitory synapses and provides an anchor to which E3 can be recruited to initiate the degradation of Gephyrin.
source: As with tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-PhoCl2c, tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-HaloTag will both label inhibitory synapses and provide an anchor to which E3 can be recruited to initiate the degradation of Gephyrin.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: Incubation of neurons expressing chGFE3 with TH for 4 hr showed a reduction of Gephyrin by 73% ± 3%.
source: Incubation of the neurons with TH for 4 hr showed a reduction of Gephyrin by 73% ± 3% (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, Figure 6B–E, n = 12 cells, 3 experiments) and a decrease in GPHN.FingR puncta by 53 ± 7% (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, n = 12 cells, 3 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6B–E.

claim: Incubating neurons expressing chGFE3 with TH for 24 hr reduced total Gephryin labeling by 89 ± 2%.
source: Incubating the neurons with TH for 24 hr reduced total Gephryin labeling by 89 ± 2%, a significant reduction (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, n = 12 cells, 3 experiments Figure 6F–I) and the number of GPHN.FingR puncta by 92 ± 0.1% (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon, n = 12 cells, 3 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6F–I.

claim: Neurons transfected with tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-HaloTag and SnapTag-E3 and treated with TH showed nonsignificant increases in labeling with GPHN.FingR.
source: To verify that Gephyrin loss depends on the dimerization between the GPHN.FingR and RINGXIAP neurons were transfected with tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-HaloTag and SnapTag-E3 and treated with TH. There were nonsignificant increases in labeling with GPHN.FingR (+20 ± 16%, p > 0.5, Wilcoxon, n = 8, 2 experiments), and the number of GPHN.FingR puncta (+11 ± 10%, p > 0.99, Wilcoxon, n = 9, 2 experiments, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: chGFE3 mediates efficient chemically induced degradation of Gephyrin.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with chGFE3 mediating efficient chemically induced degradation of Gephyrin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-Halotag/eDHFR-E3/TH complex dissociates with the addition of excess TMP.
source: The tagRFP-GPHN.FingR-Halotag/eDHFR-E3/TH complex should dissociate with the addition of excess TMP and reverse chGFE3 (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text and is illustrated in Figure 6J.

claim: Treatment of neurons expressing chGFE3 with TH for 24 hr led to a reduction of 83 ± 4% in GPHN.FingR-HaloTag labeling.
source: To test whether chGFE3 is reversible, we transfected cultured cortical neurons with GPHN.FingR-HaloTag and eDHFR-RING and treated with TH for 24 hr to induce degradation of Gephyrin, which led to a reduction of 83 ± 4% in GPHN.FingR-HaloTag labeling and 91 ± 2% reduction in the number of GPHN.FingR puncta (Figure 6K, L, N, p < 0.0001 for both, Friedman test, multiple comparisons, n = 10 cells, 2 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6K, L, N.

claim: Adding 100 µM TMP to neurons expressing chGFE3 for 24 hr after treatment with TH showed a 1450 ± 760% increase in the total GPHN.FingR labeling.
source: We then added 100 µM TMP to the media for 24 hr to compete with TH to dissociate GPHN.FingR-RINGXIAP dimers and block the formation of new dimers (Figure 6M). Imaging the neurons 48 hr after adding TMP later showed a 1450 ± 760% increase in the total GPHN.FingR labeling and 1168 ± 200% increase in Gephyrin puncta at 72 hr, which are significant (p < 0.05 for both, Friedman multiple comparison, Figure 6M and N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6M and N.

claim: The amount of GPHN.FingR labeling at 72 hr compared to labeling at T0 was reduced by 24 ± 5%, which was not significant.
source: The amount of GPHN.FingR labeling at 72 hr compared to labeling at T0 was reduced by 24 ± 5% and the number of GPHN.FingR puncta decreased by 21 ± 4%, both of which were not significant (p > 0.2, Friedman multiple comparison, Figure 6K, M, N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6K, M, N.

claim: Immunocytochemistry shows colocalization between the GPHN.FingR and the GABAA receptor after recovery from chGFE3 treatment.
source: Furthermore, immunocytochemistry shows colocalization between the GPHN.FingR and the GABAA receptor, the main ionotropic GABA receptor (Goetz et al., 2007), denoting a functional synapse (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, and is supported by a citation to Goetz et al., 2007.

claim: The Gephyrin puncta before and after ablation with chGFE3 had similar distributions across dendrites.
source: Finally, we found that the Gephyrin puncta before and after ablation had similar distributions across dendrites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In neurons expressing chGFE3, adding TH causes ablation of inhibitory neurons, and adding TMP reverses the effect.
source: Thus, our results suggest that in neurons expressing chGFE3, adding TH causes ablation of inhibitory neurons, and adding TMP reverses the effect.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PFE3 is composed of three distinct functional domains: the E3 ligase Mdm2, the PIR domain, and PSD-95.FingR.
source: PFE3 is composed of three distinct functional domains. The E3 ligase Mdm2 mediates the ubiquitination of PSD-95; the PIR domain recruits proteasomes to the synapse to degrade the ubiquitinated protein, and both domains are targeted to PSD-95 through PSD-95.FingR.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: The design of PFE3 is based on work showing that coordinated actions of Mdm2 and PIR from PCDH 10 mediate the degradation of excitatory synapses.
source: Its design is based on work showing that coordinated actions of Mdm2 and PIR from PCDH 10 mediate the degradation of excitatory synapses (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: Efficient degradation of PSD-95 and ablation of synapses was only achieved if all three components were included in PFE3.
source: These findings were corroborated when we found efficient degradation of PSD-95 and ablation of synapses was only achieved if all three components were included in PFE3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of PFE3 caused highly efficient ablation of PSD-95 in cultured cortical neurons.
source: Expression of PFE3 caused highly efficient ablation of PSD-95 in cultured cortical neurons and blocked excitatory synaptic transmission in retinal ganglion cells in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of PFE3 blocked excitatory synaptic transmission in retinal ganglion cells in vivo.
source: Expression of PFE3 caused highly efficient ablation of PSD-95 in cultured cortical neurons and blocked excitatory synaptic transmission in retinal ganglion cells in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Efficient elimination of excitatory synapses was achieved after 48 hr of PFE3 expression.
source: Efficient elimination of excitatory synapses was achieved after 48 hr of PFE3 expression, which contrasts with PSD-95 knockout mice, where reductions in AMPA receptors and excitatory transmission were either not significant or small depending on the stage of development.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In PSD-95 knockout mice, reductions in AMPA receptors and excitatory transmission were either not significant or small depending on the stage of development.
source: Efficient elimination of excitatory synapses was achieved after 48 hr of PFE3 expression, which contrasts with PSD-95 knockout mice, where reductions in AMPA receptors and excitatory transmission were either not significant or small depending on the stage of development.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: Transcription of the MAGUK protein SAP-102 is upregulated in PSD-95 knockout mice.
source: One reason for this discrepancy could be that transcription of the MAGUK protein SAP-102, which is highly homologous to PSD-95, is upregulated in PSD-95 knockout mice and could provide compensation (Coley and Gao, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coley and Gao, 2019.

claim: PSD-95.FingR labels SAP-102.
source: PSD-95.FingR labels SAP-1023, which suggests that PFE3 would degrade any SAP-102 that might otherwise compensate for the reduction in PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: PFE3 would degrade any SAP-102 that might otherwise compensate for the reduction in PSD-95.
source: PSD-95.FingR labels SAP-1023, which suggests that PFE3 would degrade any SAP-102 that might otherwise compensate for the reduction in PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The binding of PSD-95.FingR to MAGUKs homologous to PSD-95, such as SAP-102 and SAP97, could enable more effective and widespread ablation of excitatory synapses than if it bound only to PSD-95.
source: Thus, in the context of PFE3, the binding of PSD-95.FingR to MAGUKs homologous to PSD-95, such as SAP-102 and SAP97, could enable more effective and widespread ablation of excitatory synapses than if it bound only to PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three tools (PFE3, paGFE3, chGFE3) ablate specific postsynaptic sites and can be expressed in particular cell types.
source: All three tools ablate specific postsynaptic sites and can be expressed in particular cell types, allowing circuit breaking with twofold specificity.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.

claim: PFE3, paGFE3, and chGFE3 allow circuit breaking with twofold specificity.
source: All three tools ablate specific postsynaptic sites and can be expressed in particular cell types, allowing circuit breaking with twofold specificity.
evidence: The claim is stated as a direct assertion in the manuscript text.
